passages.t: One creature of clay to another
passages.happening:
“But now, O Job, hear my speech, and listen to all my words” (verse 1). His words come from an upright heart. “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life” (verse 4). Job may answer if he can. “I am just like you before God; I was also formed from clay” (verse 6). Job need not fear him.

Then Elihu quotes Job: that he is pure and without sin, yet God counts him an enemy and puts his feet in the stocks. “Behold, you are not right in this matter. I will answer you, for God is greater than man. Why do you complain to Him that He answers nothing a man asks?” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Elihu turns from the friends to Job himself. Job had demanded that God answer him and had longed for someone to stand between them (9:33; 16:19-21). Elihu takes up both. He offers himself as a fellow creature of clay who will not overwhelm Job, and he argues that God has not been silent at all.

His claim of authority is not age but the breath of the Almighty that gives life to every person, recalling the breath God breathed into the first man.

He quotes Job's words back to him, drawing on earlier speeches (13:24, 27). Some readers note that he quotes selectively. Job never claimed to be sinless; he claimed to be innocent of the charges.
passages.later: Elihu's words about God's breath recall the making of the first man, when God ‘breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being’ (Genesis 2:7).
passages.asks: Elihu offered himself as a fellow creature, no greater than Job. Ask whether you speak to people in pain as an equal or from above. And ask whether you have quoted someone's words back to them in a way that missed what they meant.

passages.t: God speaks in dreams and in pain
passages.happening:
“For God speaks in one way and in another, yet no one notices” (verse 14). In a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falls, ‘He opens their ears and terrifies them with warnings to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride, to preserve his soul from the Pit’ (verses 16-18).

‘A man is also chastened on his bed with pain and constant distress in his bones’ (verse 19). He loathes his food. His flesh wastes away until his bones stick out. ‘He draws near to the Pit, and his life to the messengers of death’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Dreams were widely treated in the ancient world as channels of divine warning. Eliphaz had already described a terrifying night vision (4:12-17). Elihu takes the idea in a gentler direction: the dream is a warning meant to turn a person back from pride.

His second picture, the sick man wasting away toward the Pit, reflects a world without modern medicine, where serious illness was often life-threatening and was often read as a sign of God's displeasure. The Pit, shachat, is a name for the grave, and it appears five times in this chapter. Elihu's point is that God's warnings aim to keep a person from going down to it and to bring them back to the light.
passages.hard:
Elihu says God may speak through sickness. Can anyone say that of a particular person's illness?

Elihu's idea is not the friends' idea. He does not say that Job's suffering proves past sin. He says suffering can be God's merciful warning and discipline, meant to save. Scripture does speak of God teaching through hardship, and many believers have looked back on illness and found that they learned something there.

But Elihu does not claim that anyone can tell what God is doing in a particular case, and the book as a whole warns against reading any particular disaster as a verdict on the person it strikes. Job's own children died in a storm (1:19), and the reader knows it was not their punishment. And Elihu still does not know what the reader knows from the prologue, that Job was tested precisely because he was blameless.

No one may tell a sick person that their illness is God's warning to them. Whatever may be true of God's purposes, it is not for anyone else to read them from the outside.
passages.asks: Elihu believed God speaks in more ways than people notice. Ask what God may have taught you in a hard season, looking back. And ask whether you have ever presumed to explain to another person what God was teaching them through their pain.

passages.t: A messenger on his side, and a ransom
passages.happening:
‘Yet if there is a messenger on his side, one mediator in a thousand, to tell a man what is right for him, to be gracious to him’ (verses 23-24), and to say that he should be spared from the Pit because a ransom has been found, ‘then his flesh is refreshed like a child’s; he returns to the days of his youth’ (verse 25).

He prays to God and finds favor. He sees God's face and shouts for joy. Then he sings before others: “I have sinned and perverted what was right; yet I did not get what I deserved. He redeemed my soul from going down to the Pit, and I will live to see the light” (verses 27-28).

God does all this two or three times, to bring a soul back from the Pit. Elihu asks Job to listen, and to answer if he can: ‘speak up, for I would like to vindicate you’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Job had lamented that there was no mediator between him and God. Elihu describes one. The word for mediator here, from luts, means an interpreter or go-between, someone who speaks for another. Interpreters debate whether Elihu means an angel, a human teacher who explains God's ways, or a figure left undefined. The word allows each.

Ransom, kopher, means a price paid to release a life that would otherwise be lost. In verse 24 the ransom is found for the sufferer, not produced by him, which makes the rescue an act of grace.

The passage ends in a small drama: suffering, a messenger who pleads, restoration, and a song of thanks sung in front of others.

There is something kind in Elihu's last words. He says he would like to find Job in the right.
passages.later: The same word for a go-between is used of the man who interpreted between Joseph and his brothers: ‘there was an interpreter between them’ (Genesis 42:23). And the law used the word ransom for the price that spared a life (Exodus 30:12).
passages.asks: Elihu pictured someone standing beside a dying man to plead for him. Ask who has stood beside you in that way. And ask for whom you could be one in a thousand.
